@foysalemonshanto @jakobbrggen — one specific observation, not a mass ping.

As of today the leaderboard shows 1.61 three times: rank 5, 6 and 7. Your two teams posted the same score as the team inside the prize band; what separates you from it is submission timing, not performance. Leaderboard prizes stop at top 5, so as it stands that score pays nothing there.

The Paper Track still counts it. Its rubric weighs leaderboard accuracy alongside the write-up, and I have a finished, submitted methods paper on ARC-AGI-3's scoring — with a 0.79 score, which is exactly the axis I'm weak on. Your score plus my paper is one entry that isn't weak on either.

To be straight about the cost, same as in the post above: the paper currently documents a measurement, not a solver, and the rubric asks how thoroughly it covers your submission — so it would need substantial rework. That work would be mine, not yours. And I'm not pretending the odds are good; my own estimate is roughly one in three or four for a top-three place as a merged team.

Even split by default, negotiable. Merger deadline is Oct 26, and combined submission counts are nowhere near the cap.

If it's not for you, no reply needed — I won't follow up. Happy to send the paper first to anyone who'd rather judge it before deciding.

firstMessage.rawMarkdown:
I'm looking for a team-up for the ARC Prize 2026 Paper Track, and I'd rather be
blunt about what I bring and what I don't.

**What I don't bring:** a competitive ARC-AGI-3 score. I'm at 0.79 from a single
submission — the Duck harness at `n_passes = 1`, which is the configuration my
experiment required, not one aimed at the leaderboard. You can see exactly where
that puts me on the board.

**What I bring:** a finished, pre-registered write-up that measures the
ARC-AGI-3 score instead of trying to beat it. It works from the 500 published
game-runs of the Milestone-1 harness — 25 games × 20 repetitions of one fixed
configuration, so the spread across them is pure repetition noise.

Three findings, so you can judge whether this is worth your time rather than
taking my word for it:

**1. The score is dominated by a binary term.** 84.7 % of the repetition variance
comes from "did the agent clear level *n* or not" (bootstrap 95 % CI [78.5,
91.1]); only 15.3 % comes from the efficiency term the formula spends most of its
complexity on. The mechanism is downstream cancellation in the sequential level
structure: failing early erases every later level at once, which turns a modest
per-level success probability into a heavy-tailed score.

**2. The variance is concentrated in almost nothing.** Two of the 25 public games
carry 65 % of the total variance — one game alone carries 49.8 % — while two
games contribute exactly zero. Half of all 500 runs score exactly 0; the mean is
1.60 and the maximum 25.33.

**3. `n_passes: 20` does not fit in a Kaggle notebook.** The harness ships with
that default. Measured on my own run — 25 games, one pass, single RTX 6000, GPU
saturated at 193 generated tokens/s throughout — one pass costs about 124 minutes
of play plus 8 minutes of model loading, with all 25 games running concurrently.
Against the 9-hour notebook limit that is roughly four passes, not twenty. The
published 500-run artefact was produced under a deployment config declaring two
B200s and a 13-hour window. If you have been reading the winner's configuration
as a recipe, it is a recipe for different hardware. (Measured under my settings;
a shorter per-game budget trades depth for passes, which is its own decision.)

There is more in the write-up — a significance analysis of the leaderboard's rank
structure against the correct null, and a pre-registered causal experiment on
disclosing the scoring function to the agent, reported as inconclusive because
that is what it is — but posting those details before the deadline would rather
defeat the point of entering.

**Why this has to be a merger.** The Paper Track rules require the write-up's team
to match the team that made the ARC-AGI-3 submission. A paper can only document a
score its own team achieved, so I cannot simply write about someone else's work.
The team merger deadline is 26 October.

**The arithmetic.** As of 5 August, 118 teams have entered the Paper Track;
2,065 are on the ARC-AGI-3 leaderboard. The final leaderboard prizes stop at
fifth place, so if you are outside the top five your score currently earns
nothing — while the Paper Track pays $75,000 across three places in a field one
twentieth the size. Most strong teams never write anything up.

**What it would cost you.** Kaggle allocates prizes in even shares among team
members unless the team unanimously agrees otherwise and notifies Kaggle before
payout, so the split is negotiable but even by default. And the write-up would
need substantial rework: the rubric asks how thoroughly the paper covers *your*
submission, and mine currently covers a measurement, not a solver. That is real
work and I would be the one doing it.

I am not going to pretend the odds are good. The rubric rewards leaderboard
accuracy and progress toward actually solving ARC, and a measurement paper is
weak on both. My own estimate is somewhere around one in three or four for a
top-three place as a merged team, against roughly one in twenty on my own —
judge that estimate yourself, I can show you how I got there.

If any of the three findings above were new to you, that is about the value I
would be bringing. Reply here if you want to talk.
